Himalayan Linguistics 22(1): 202-242. doi:10.5070/H922159463. [PDF imprint: 'Himalayan Linguistics, Vol. 22(1). (c) Himalayan Linguistics 2023'; eScholarship publication date 2023; Crossref issued date 2022-07-31]
tone_statements.quote: The Vaiphei examples are supplied by the fourth author and are presented in the orthography used in Pathian Lekhabu Thiangtho 2006. Tones are marked only on verb forms; the system of marking tones is as in Lai: an acute accent [´] represents rising tone, a grave accent [`] represents falling tone, and unmarked represents low tone.
tone_statements.summary: Three tones marked on Vaiphei verbs (rising, falling, low); stem alternation involves tone change plus final-consonant change; no tonal analysis beyond the marking convention.

tone_statements.citation: Suantak, Khawlsonkim. 2013. Vaiphei phonetics, phonology and morphology: a descriptive study. PhD thesis, Department of Linguistics, North-Eastern Hill University, Shillong. xi+284 pp. Shodhganga hdl 10603/169680.
tone_statements.quote: Vaiphei is a tonal language like other related Tibeto-Burman languages. … This analysis proposes that Vaiphei has three contrastive tones, two contour tones (rising and falling) and a low tone. … In the study, the Chao tone number system (used in the International Phonetic Alphabet) is used to transcribe phonetic surface tones. Tone 1 Low 21 Tone 2 Rising 23 Tone 3 Falling 52 … In Vaiphei, all the three tones low, rising and falling occur on both open and closed syllables.
tone_statements.locator: pp.116-117, sec. 4.8.1 'Tone System' and p.119, sec. 4.8.2 'Tone Contrasts'

tone.locator: pp.116-117, sec. 4.8.1 'Tone System' and p.119, sec. 4.8.2 'Tone Contrasts'
tone.says: Three contrastive tones on the syllable: low (21), rising (23) and falling (52); rising and falling do not occur before final glottal stop; low becomes rising after a rising tone in compounds.

sources.note: Phonology section (from Suantak 2013): consonants, vowels, three tones (21, 23, 52), tone sandhi, (C)V(C) syllable; nothing on stress or accent.

sources.citation: Lotven, Samson. 2023. Tone in South Central Tibeto-Burman (Kuki-Chin) [survey text held under reng1255].
sources.note: Cites Suantak 2013 only for Vaiphei tone facts (L on all syllable shapes, no contours before glottal stop, p.121; L -> Rise as first member of compound, p.122; tonal stem alternation). Nothing on Vaiphei stress.

sources.citation: Prichard, Jesse. 2018. Verb Stem Alternation in Vaiphei. MA thesis, Portland State University (Dissertations and Theses 4470). doi:10.15760/etd.6354. 94 pp.
sources.note: No word-stress statement. Only 'vocalic stress' within diphthongs after Button (2011): 'The vocalic stress in diphthongs of the cognate pia in Vaiphei matches that of Sizang and Thadou, but not that of Zo and Teddim' (p.58), i.e. which element of a diphthong is prominent; recommends a future 'study of vocalic stress assignment in Vaiphei' (p.7). Phonology otherwise taken from Suantak 2010/2013 (tones, phonotactics).

sources.citation: Yumnam, Satyabati Devi. 2010. A comparative phonology of Hmar, Paite and Vaiphei. PhD thesis, Department of Linguistics, Manipur University. 271 pp. Shodhganga hdl 10603/105257 (scanned).

Only level tone is marked by (-)' (p.194); conclusion (p.226) repeats '2 suprasegmental phonemes are Level tone and Falling tone'. No stress/accent statement in TOC, tone/syllable pages or conclusion.

sources.note: Not a tone study: a morphosyntactic survey of base~derived verb stems in Lai, K'Cho and Vaiphei. Its tone content for Vaiphei is (i) the transcription statement on p.203 that Vaiphei verb forms carry a three-way tone marking (acute = rising, grave = falling, unmarked = low), consistent with Suantak 2013's three tones, (ii) tone-marked Vaiphei base~derived verb pairs throughout sections 2.3-13.3 (e.g. túng ~ tùn 'arrive', imú ~ imùt 'sleep', p.205), and (iii) the remark (p.206) that Vaiphei derived-stem formation has not been studied to the level of Lai, so no rules (tonal or segmental) are of…
